So today, I am delighted to be able to interview one of the researchers who is on the cusp
of making a medical breakthrough that will positively affect all women around the world.
Wow, that is amazing to consider isn't it? I mean, all women around the world could be
positively impacted by this research. So Dr Harritt's, welcome. It is an honour to have you here.
Thank you for the invitation. It is certainly a privilege to be here to share with all of your
listeners the research that I've been working on for much of my professional life. So most of you
have probably seen the headline saying that a simple blood test for early detection of breast cancer
is in development. So today that's exactly what we are going to learn more about with Dr Harris here.
So Dr Harris, how is this even possible? Simple blood test?
Yes, a simple blood test. So cancer cells produce proteins called antigens. These antigens trigger
the body to make antibodies against them, auto-antibodies. So, we realised that these
tumour-associated antigens are good indicators of cancer, and so we started to work on developing
panels of tumour-associated antigens that are already known to be associated with breast cancer.
Yes, this is a pilot study that your research did at the University of Nottingham, correct?
And correct. We took blood samples from 90 breast cancer patients at the time they were
diagnosed with breast cancer and matched them with samples taken from 90 patients without
breast cancer. We used screening technology that allowed us to screen the blood samples
rapidly for the presence of antibodies against 40 tumor-associated antigens associated with
breast cancer, as well as against 27 tumor-associated antigens not linked with the disease.
So what was the result of that pilot study?
Well, the results of the study showed that breast cancer does induce autoantibodies against
panels of specific tumor-associated antigens.
We were indeed able to detect cancer with reasonable accuracy by identifying these autoantibodies
in the blood.
Hmm, what do you mean when you say reasonable accuracy?
Well, it is important to mention that we identified three panels of tumor-associated antigens to test for antibodies.
We found that the accuracy of the test improved in the panels that contained more antibodies.
For example, the panel of five tumor-associated antigens correctly detected breast cancer in 29% of the samples from cancer patients
currently identified 84% of the control samples being cancer free, but the panel of seven tumor
associated antigens correctly identified cancer in 35% of cancer samples and no cancer in 79% of
control samples. Finally, the panel of nine antigens correctly identified cancer in 37% of
cancer samples and no cancer in 79% of the controls.
Interesting, there was a much bigger jump in accuracy between the panels with 5 and 7
tumour-associated antigens than between 7 and 9.
Yes, that is true. We are working to develop and further validate this test. We are currently
working on testing the 9 tumour-associated antigen panel with samples from 800 patients.
is definitely needed. But these results are so encouraging. I mean, they mean that there
is a possibility of detecting a signal of early breast cancer.
